not_modelled.what: The 24,000/48,000 subtraction (Schedule SB line 16) bars every Wisconsin credit for the year: Schedule CR and Form 1 lines 13-20 and 30-35 (itemized deduction credit, school property tax credit up to 300, married couple credit up to 480, credit for net tax paid to another state, earned income credit, homestead credit and others), and credit carryforwards. The filer chooses the better of the subtraction or the credits. The projection models none of these credits, so it always takes the subtraction: right whenever the subtraction is worth more, which is the usual case; when the credits are worth more the filer would skip the subtraction, and the projection overstates tax by the difference.

Wisconsin credits are not modelled: itemized deduction credit (5% of certain federal itemized deductions over the Wisconsin standard deduction), school property tax credit (renters and homeowners, at most 300), married couple credit (3% of the smaller spouse's qualified earned income, at most 480), credit for net tax paid to another state, homestead credit, earned income credit and Schedule CR credits. Leaving them out overstates tax for a household that would claim them and does not claim the 24,000/48,000 subtraction.

Payments from seven listed Milwaukee and Wisconsin State Teachers systems and the federal Civil Service Retirement System are exempt when the account was established before 1964 (retired before 1964, a member on December 31, 1963, or a beneficiary of such a person); the projection taxes them, as it does not know the membership date.
Disability income exclusion of up to 5,200 for a person under 65 retired on permanent and total disability, federal AGI under 20,200 (25,400 if married and both eligible).

Interest on U.S. government obligations (not Ginnie Mae) is subtracted, and so is the part of an IRA or plan distribution attributable to U.S. government securities interest (Publication 126 worksheet).
Pre-1965 school-system tax-sheltered annuities on which Wisconsin tax was already paid (certain retired teachers).
U.S. Armed Forces active duty pay is subtracted.
Long-term gains on farm assets take a 60% exclusion instead of 30%.
Standard deduction of a filer who can be claimed as someone else's dependent (earned income plus 450, at least 1,350, at most the table amount).
Wisconsin penalty of 33% of the federal penalty tax on early IRA and retirement plan distributions (Form 1 line 25), for example 3.3% of an early distribution that pays the federal 10% tax.
A lump-sum distribution reported on federal Form 4972 is added to Wisconsin income as ordinary income (Schedule AD line 6).

approximations.what: Joint return where only one spouse is 67 or older: the projection applies the 48,000 joint cap to that spouse's own qualifying income; Wisconsin allows 24,000 then (48,000 only when both are 67). A joint return where both are 67 is exact, which is why the joint cap is used.
approximations.size: Only when the 67-or-older spouse has more than 24,000 of qualifying income in the years before the other turns 67: at most 24,000 x 5.3% = 1,272 a year (1,836 at 7.65%).

approximations.what: The projection always takes the 24,000/48,000 subtraction for a person 67 or older, never the Wisconsin credits it bars (see not_modelled); a household whose credits are worth more would skip it.
approximations.size: At most the credits given up less the subtraction's tax value. Example: 3,000 of IRA income saves 3,000 x 5.3% = 159, against a school property tax credit of up to 300.

approximations.what: Roth conversions are left out of both retirement subtractions (covers_unclear: the booklets do not say whether a conversion counts, though the 5,000 worksheet takes federal Form 1040 line 4b).
approximations.size: 5.3% of the conversion, up to the room left in the 24,000 (48,000 joint) subtraction, for a person 67 or older in a conversion year: up to 1,272 a year (2,544 joint).

approximations.what: Annuity income is counted in both retirement subtractions; Wisconsin counts annuity income only from a qualified retirement plan or IRA, so an annuity bought outside a plan would not qualify.
approximations.size: 5.3% of a non-plan annuity, up to the subtraction's room: up to 1,272 a year per person.

approximations.what: The 5,000 subtraction takes only retirement income left after the 24,000/48,000 subtraction; the projection applies each to the full covered income.
approximations.size: Small: the 5,000 needs federal AGI under 15,000 (30,000 joint), where the standard deduction and exemptions take almost everything left. Roughly 100 a year at most.

approximations.what: Married filing separately: the 5,000 subtraction's income test is the sum of both spouses' federal AGI; the projection uses the filer's own.
approximations.size: At most 5,000 x 4.4% = 220 a year, only for a separate filer 65 or older whose spouse has income.

approximations.what: Municipal interest is all treated as taxed. Wisconsin taxes its own municipal bonds as well as other states', except 18 listed kinds (bonds of named Wisconsin authorities and districts, and bonds of Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa), which are exempt.
approximations.size: Up to 7.65% of interest from the listed exempt bonds; nothing for ordinary Wisconsin or other-state municipal bonds.

approximations.what: A qualifying surviving spouse files as head of household in Wisconsin (Form 1 Instructions page 13); the projection's default for that status is the married-joint schedule and deduction.
approximations.size: About 130 a year at 60,000 of taxable income from the schedule alone, plus the larger joint standard deduction; more at higher incomes.

approximations.what: The standard deduction is taken for every return, and the itemized deduction credit is not modelled (Wisconsin has no itemized deduction).
approximations.size: 5% of the household's qualifying itemized deductions over the Wisconsin standard deduction.

approximations.what: Wisconsin starts from federal AGI adjusted on Schedule I for federal law Wisconsin has not adopted (Form 1 line 2; the Schedule I instructions are not in the sources); the projection uses federal AGI as is.
approximations.size: Usually nothing for a retirement household.

approximations.what: The 30% long-term gain exclusion is applied to long-term gains as the projection holds them; Schedule WD's netting, holding-period and loss rules are not in the sources.
approximations.size: Only with losses or short-term gains in the same year.
